claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys is controlled by the interplay between local chemical ordering and lattice distortions.
Local chemical ordering and lattice distortions modulate defect energetics.
The proposed ordering–distortion interaction produces a balanced multiphase microstructure.
A balanced multiphase microstructure underpins high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Nominally equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni made by standard synthesis has a characteristic mixture of ordered and disordered phases.
Changing alloy composition can alter local chemical ordering and the magnitude of lattice distortions.
Differences in atomic size and electronegativity create local chemical ordering and associated lattice distortions.
Ordering-induced lattice distortions affect defect formation and propagation energetics.
Ordering and lattice distortions determine the relative fractions of ordered, disordered, or other phase regions.
Changes in ordered and disordered phase fractions stabilize the microstructure and influence mechanical and environmental performance.
An optimized level of local chemical ordering will produce a more stable multiphase structure than the equiatomic baseline.
Greater multiphase stability will correlate with improved high-temperature strength.
Greater multiphase stability will correlate with improved corrosion resistance.
Greater multiphase stability will correlate with enhanced radiation tolerance, manifested as lower defect density.
Greater multiphase stability will correlate with superior cryogenic toughness.
Both insufficient and excessive local ordering will degrade the proposed balance of properties.
The equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni baseline has known ordered and disordered phases and established property benchmarks.
The proposed mechanism is limited to conventional processing and compositional ranges in which atomic-size mismatch and chemical-ordering effects are significant.
Extreme compositional deviations or nontraditional processing may produce different behavior.
Failure of composition-induced changes in ordering and distortion to correlate with phase fractions or the specified properties would falsify the hypothesis.
